SEALED · EARN 3 SIGILS IN THIS SANCTUARY
The first ring was cut from a single slab of quarry marble and set on a bronze bed that still turns without complaint. Priests called it the patient wheel, because it waits centuries between hands.
Sea air crept under the sanctuary doors for nine hundred winters. The green bloom on every clamp is not decay but armour, and the machine wears it the way an old soldier wears scars.
At the centre sits a sphere of fused storm glass that has never once gone dark. Hold a palm near it and the hair on your arm lifts, as if the thing remembers what it was built to carry.
The builders discharged the machine only once in their lifetimes. Witnesses wrote that the light did not flash but poured, slow and heavy, like gold leaving a crucible.
Each clamp carries the mark of the smith who forged it. Twelve marks repeat across the sanctuary, which means twelve people spent their working lives on a machine none of them would ever see fire.
Deeper rings were poured, not carved. Molten bronze was run into marble moulds so the channel and its shell cooled as one body, and nothing since has been able to prise them apart.
Some sectors were left blind on purpose. A machine that could be solved by brute turning was considered unworthy of the storm it was meant to hold.
Charge was never free. Every turn of a ring draws from a reservoir that the sanctuary refills on its own schedule, and the schedule has never been explained to anyone outside the order.
When two rings lock in the same breath the whole hall hums a low note. Old keepers insisted the machine was thanking them, and nobody has produced a better explanation.
Hint crystals are grown, not found. Fragments of a powered gate are laid on a cold stone bed and left until the storm residue inside them finds a shape it likes.
The upper sanctuary stands above the cloud line. Lightning strikes its outer shell forty times a season, and the shell has never needed a repair.
At the apex the channel must feed two gates from one core. The builders solved it by making the outer ring wider than any other, so the current splits exactly where it must.
Thin scratches run along the apex rim at intervals no instrument explains. They match no calendar, no star, and no tide, and the order simply calls them the counting.
Every powered gate has opened onto the same thing: a corridor of still air, warm as a hand, with no end that anyone has walked to and returned from.
The final entry in the sanctuary ledger is a single line in a steady hand. It reads that the machine is sound, that the charge is full, and that whoever comes next should take their time.
Three clean runs through the first hall mark you as a reader of channels rather than a turner of stone. The order stamped that distinction into a gold sigil and nothing else.
Mastery of the bronze halls was measured in restraint. Three gates powered inside par meant the candidate had learned to spend charge the way a smith spends heat.
No name survives of anyone who took three apex sigils. The ledger records only that the hall was found empty, the gates open, and every clamp seated.
